title: Songbook and Orchard
premise: Ada Voss inherited Voss Orchard Vineyard buried in debt, and for twenty years she has lived small, hiding the truth about the fire that nearly killed her business partner Elias Thorne and ended her engagement to his brother, Julian. When a snowstorm traps Ada, Elias, and Julian together in the orchard's crumbling farmhouse, twenty years of silence collapse: Elias has returned dying, seeking confession; Julian has returned as the lawyer representing the bank foreclosing on her land. Over six snowbound days, Ada must choose between protecting her carefully rebuilt identity and telling the truth that could save the orchard but destroy both brothers' loyalty to each other. She ends by confessing publicly at the foreclosure hearing, forgiving herself, and choosing neither man until she can stand as herself—though the final chapter leaves the door open with Julian, who chooses truth over the firm.
about_author: Mirabel Dunmore is the pen name of a former sommelier who spent a decade working family vineyards in the Finger Lakes before turning to fiction. Her novels explore how people forgive themselves last, and she still prunes grapes every spring 'to keep the metaphors honest.'

chapters.title: Bare Canes
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Winter pruning on the edge of bankruptcy; Ada counts debts like frost damage and rehearses the small safe life she's built. A letter arrives from the bank with a foreclosure date. Emotional beat: dread disguised as routine, establishing what she stands to lose.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed Nothing
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian arrives in town as counsel for Meridian Bank, assigned to the Voss foreclosure he requested—or so his firm believes. He tells himself it's closure, not obsession. Emotional beat: guilt wearing a tailored coat; he hasn't seen Ada in twenty years.

chapters.title: What the Storm Knew First
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The forecast turns; Ada drives to town for supplies and collides—literally—with Julian in the hardware store. Their first exchange is all invoices and ice. Emotional beat: the shock of recognition, anger arriving before grief does.

chapters.title: Elias Comes Home
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias returns unannounced, thinner, carrying a locked satchel and a doctor's letter he doesn't open. He asks Ada for shelter through the storm, saying only, 'I owe you a fire.' Emotional beat: tenderness laced with terminal urgency.

chapters.title: Three Plates
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The storm closes the road; Julian, stranded after coming to serve papers, takes the farmhouse's third room. Dinner is a minefield of twenty-year-old silences. Emotional beat: forced intimacy, the past setting the table whether anyone wants it or not.

chapters.title: The Night of the Fire, As Told Wrong
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian recounts the official story—the electrical fault, Ada's negligence claim, the settlement that broke the engagement. Elias listens and says nothing. Ada leaves the room. Emotional beat: the reader senses the record is wrong; loyalty and truth begin pulling apart.

chapters.title: Cellar Inventory
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada and Elias inventory the cellar by lantern light; he reveals he's sick and that he came to confess before he dies—but not yet, not all at once. Emotional beat: two people keeping the same secret from different ends of it.

chapters.title: Snowbound Ledger
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian finds discrepancies in the old fire investigation file he brought as leverage—and realizes the numbers were doctored, possibly by his own firm's predecessor. Emotional beat: the lawyer discovering the law was the first thing broken.

chapters.title: The Best Mistake of Our Twenties
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Flashback chapter: the night of the fire, told truly—Elias set it himself, burning the fraudulent contracts he'd signed with a predatory distributor, and let the world blame an accident while Ada took the financial ruin. Emotional beat: confession withheld, guilt made flesh.

chapters.title: What Ada Carried Out
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Second flashback: Ada knew Elias set the fire—she saw him that night—and chose silence to protect him, losing Julian, her name, and her own self-respect in one winter. Emotional beat: the person in the mirror becomes the hardest witness.

chapters.title: Thaw Lines
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian and Ada, unable to sleep, talk honestly for the first time—not about the fire, but about the years between. Something tender and dangerous rekindles. Emotional beat: forgiveness attempted out of order, before the truth that requires it.

chapters.title: The Satchel
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada finds Elias's satchel open: medical records, a written confession, and proof the distributor's fraud would have destroyed the orchard anyway. She must decide whether to reveal it or honor his timing. Emotional beat: loyalty versus truth, held in both hands.

chapters.title: Julian's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. The bank offers Julian a partnership if the foreclosure proceeds cleanly; pursuing the fraud evidence means burning his career. He drafts two letters—one resignation, one recommendation—and burns neither. Emotional beat: ambition measured against conscience.

chapters.title: Elias Collapses
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Elias collapses in the vineyard rows during a brief thaw; the storm has them trapped with no hospital for miles. Ada keeps him alive through the night while Julian reads aloud from the orchard's old songbook to steady them all. Emotional beat: mortality stripping pretense away.

chapters.title: Confession at the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias tells Julian everything—that he set the fire, that Ada covered for him, that Julian's whole grievance was built on a lie meant to protect him too. Julian walks out into the snow. Emotional beat: truth delivered like a blow meant as mercy.

chapters.title: The Person in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Alone, Ada confronts her own reflection and the twenty-year project of invisibility. She realizes forgiving Elias and Julian means nothing without forgiving herself first. Emotional beat: the novel's thematic hinge—self-forgiveness as the prerequisite for justice.

chapters.title: Julian's Choice
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian returns frozen and changed. He withdraws from the foreclosure, sends the fraud evidence to the state attorney general, and resigns from Meridian—knowing it may end his career and may not even save the orchard. Emotional beat: justice chosen outside the law's comfortable channels.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At the foreclosure hearing, before Julian's resignation lands, Ada stands and tells the whole truth herself—her silence, Elias's fire, the fraud—refusing to be saved by anyone else's sacrifice. Emotional beat: reclaiming her name in public, at maximum cost.

chapters.title: What the Law Couldn't Do
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. The AG opens an investigation; the distributor's fraud voids the underlying debt claims, and the foreclosure stalls. It isn't tidy—Elias may still face charges—but it's honest. Emotional beat: imperfect justice that costs everyone something real.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Weeks later, Ada and Elias prune the vines together while he awaits sentencing; they negotiate the terms of their forgiven friendship. The orchard will survive, smaller and truer. Emotional beat: grief and gratitude sharing the same row.

chapters.title: Songbook
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian, now independent counsel helping victims of the same distributor, comes to the orchard with the old songbook and no agenda except honesty. He and Ada begin again slowly, without promises. Emotional beat: love rebuilt on truth instead of protection.

chapters.title: First Green
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Spring bud-break; Elias, sentenced to community service served at the orchard, watches Ada graft new stock. Ada signs her full name to the new deed—Voss restored, debts paid in truth rather than silence. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope; identity reclaimed.
